video_title: The Macro Implications of the Blue Tsunami | Odd Lots
gist: Recorded November 5, 2026 after Democrats won both the House and Senate in the midterms, Skanda Amarnath of Employ America argues the Senate win matters structurally for Fed and court appointments, that Democratic governors now running the main data-center states turn state politics into a new risk for AI capex, and that energy, AI-driven hardware prices and tariffs not yet passed through could keep inflation near 3% for longer than expected. The hosts also cover the market reaction: the S&P rose while Tesla, SpaceX, Texas data-center builders and neoclouds sold off.

themes.theme: Market reaction: unwinding the 2024 Trump trade

insights.claim: Bank of America's Michael Hartnett had warned the S&P 500 could fall 10% if Democrats won the 2026 midterms, but the S&P 500 rose about 1.5% the day after the Democratic sweep.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: The well-known sell-side call that a blue sweep would hurt stocks was wrong at the index level, so the impact shows up in specific sectors and names, not the broad market.

insights.claim: The selling after the election was concentrated in names tied to Trump and Texas: Tesla fell about 10% and SpaceX about 7.5%, the Nasdaq was getting hammered on November 5, and neoclouds hoping to expand their footprint also dropped sharply.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Elon Musk-linked stocks, Texas exposure and AI infrastructure names are now trading on political risk, which marks the reversal of the post-2024 election trade.
insights.quote: Tesla shares declined 10% space for another 7%, 7.5%.

insights.claim: Skanda Amarnath describes the post-midterm selloff as unwinding the stocks that ripped after Trump won in 2024, especially companies whose leaders put a lot of money behind Trump's election.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: This gives a way to screen for more downside: look for the 2024 election winners whose gains depended on federal or Texas political alignment.
insights.quote: this unwinding of the effects from the 2024, um, election response where you had a lot of stocks that really ripped, uh, after Trump won

insights.claim: Sterling Infrastructure, which builds data centers in Texas, has a chart that Tracy Alloway compared to a dot-com bust, with the stock at roughly $255 at the time of recording after peaking in June.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Data-center construction contractors exposed to Texas are taking the hardest repricing from the political shift.
insights.quote: they build data centers in Texas, and that looks like a.com chart

insights.claim: Homebuilder stocks rose sharply the day after the election, partly because of a move in interest rates, which fits the idea that slower AI capex could mean a softer economy and lower rates that leave room for other sectors.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive sectors such as housing gain if the AI capex boom cools and rates fall, but Amarnath doubts they can fill the gap quickly.

themes.theme: Data-center politics move to Democratic statehouses

insights.claim: After the midterms, the leading states for data-center construction (Texas, Georgia, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Virginia and Wisconsin) are, by Skanda Amarnath's account, all run by Democratic governors, and most permitting and power decisions for data centers are made at the state and local level rather than the federal level.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers and AI infrastructure builders now face a new and possibly coordinated political variable in exactly the places they are building most.
insights.quote: the power related data center construction kind of resides at the state level. State and local, um, not federal.

insights.claim: If five or six governors of the same party lead the main data-center states, they could coordinate policy toward data centers, ending the era of easy tax breaks that even many blue states offered.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Data-center tax incentives and terms of power cost sharing could get worse for developers across several states at the same time.

insights.claim: OpenAI said, right after the election, that it will change how it handles data-center projects after public outcry, including no longer using NDAs and not making local residents pay for the data centers' electricity.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: AI companies are already giving ground on local terms, which points to higher all-in costs to build data centers.

insights.claim: Josh Shapiro and Greg Abbott, probably the two most pro-data-center governors, both had to pivot on the issue. Shapiro pulled it off successfully and Abbott less so, though Abbott's loss may reflect the macro environment more than his data-center messaging.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Even the friendliest politicians now treat data centers as a liability with voters, so expect pressure for smaller footprints and more concessions.

insights.claim: One trade discussed is going short the US dollar against the Malaysian ringgit, on the view that the expected compute shortage will still be met with data centers built outside the US, in places such as Malaysia.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: If US local resistance pushes compute buildout to other countries, the currencies and assets of data-center hubs such as Malaysia benefit.

insights.claim: Tighter limits on new data centers could benefit incumbent hyperscalers that already have large footprints, letting them charge more for capacity, and GPU rental prices were still rising the day after the election.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Limits on supply raise the value of existing data-center capacity and compute already in place, even as new-build plays suffer.

themes.theme: AI capex economics and the capital structure

insights.claim: Skanda Amarnath argues the economics of AI capex matter more than the politics, and that even before the election, markets had begun rewarding capital efficiency over raw capex.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Investors favor capital-light AI exposure over heavy spenders, whichever party is in power.

insights.claim: Where a company sits in the AI value chain shapes what it wants. Nvidia and Caterpillar, the picks-and-shovels suppliers, want maximum buildout. Anthropic and OpenAI must stay at the frontier but also show sustainable profitability. Hyperscalers are in an arms race where capex is a real cost to them.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: This helps tell suppliers that gain from any capex apart from spenders whose shareholders may welcome a slowdown.
insights.quote: there's a little bit bootleggers and Baptists, uh, type dynamic

insights.claim: The heavy capex is turning hyperscalers' advertising businesses, once the best business model in the world, into something that looks more like an industrial company, with the cost hitting depreciation rather than EBITDA.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: If investors start valuing big tech as capital-intensive industrials, multiples could come down.
insights.quote: what was once the best business model in the world ads, um, is now a one that looks a lot more like an industrial

insights.claim: Funding pressure from AI capex is working its way up the capital structure: hyperscalers moved from paying for capex with cash to borrowing in the bond market, and some, such as Oracle, are now issuing new equity.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Issuing equity to fund capex is a late-cycle sign of financing strain, with dilution risk for shareholders and supply pressure for credit investors.

themes.theme: Macro: an AI-led cycle with no easy offset

insights.claim: Skanda Amarnath estimates that the AI-sensitive parts of US spending (tech hardware, software and industrial equipment) are getting close to 8% of GDP, large enough that they will probably drive the business cycle.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: The path of AI capex is now the main macro variable for US growth, so a capex pullback is a recession risk, not just a sector story.
insights.quote: It's something getting close to 8% of GDP.

insights.claim: Skanda Amarnath doubts that a cooling of AI capex would be smoothly offset by another sector such as housing, because capex booms tend to switch on or off rather than fade gradually, and history suggests the Goldilocks handoff is hard to achieve.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: This argues against the soft-landing rotation trade, since an AI capex stop could produce a sharper slowdown than the consensus expects.
insights.quote: these things tend to not be very linear

insights.claim: The Fed was flagging rate cuts as late as its May meeting, which Skanda Amarnath says was too late given that the economy had already solidified once the government shutdown ended. The non-AI economy is fine but not gangbusters, and housing is still terrible.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: The 'soft non-AI economy' story was overstated, which limits how much room the Fed has to ease.

themes.theme: Sticky ~3% inflation: energy, AI hardware, tariffs

insights.claim: Skanda Amarnath sees three forces keeping US inflation elevated: energy shocks from the Strait of Hormuz closure and refining problems tied to Russia-Ukraine, durable AI-driven price increases such as memory and laptops, and tariff costs not yet passed through. They may not push inflation to 4%, but they could keep it around 3% for longer than expected.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: A sticky 3% inflation regime limits Fed cuts and supports positioning for higher-for-longer rates and inflation protection.
insights.quote: we may be stuck around three a lot longer than, um, is currently suspected

insights.claim: Hot services inflation is driven partly by airfares, which rose sharply because jet fuel prices blew out, rather than by labor-market tightness. High diesel costs could still pass through to food and food-services prices, which feed into core inflation.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Services inflation is being driven by energy costs, which changes how to read Fed reaction functions, and food retailers' margins and pricing are the next place to watch.
insights.quote: airfares are sensitive to energy. Um, it's not necessarily because of the labor market.

insights.claim: Autos are a notable category where tariff costs have not yet reached consumer prices, partly because of a different tariff regime, and a lot of the cost of the Canadian tariffs has also not yet passed through.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Car price inflation is still to come, a risk to auto demand and to inflation prints.

themes.theme: Senate control, Fed appointments and gridlock

insights.claim: Skanda Amarnath argues the Democratic Senate win matters structurally because the Senate confirms Supreme Court justices and Fed governors, and six-year terms mean even one-off wins in states like South Carolina or Mississippi tilt confirmations for four to six years.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: This makes it much harder for the president to reshape the Fed board, which lowers the risk of a politicized, overly dovish Fed.

insights.claim: If Jay Powell steps down before his term ends in early 2028, Skanda Amarnath's best guess is that the seat probably will not be filled, because the nominee would have to clear Democratic veto points unless the White House picks someone trusted Democrats can quickly back.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: The current Fed board composition is likely to stay intact, reducing the odds of a sharp shift in policy from political appointments.

insights.claim: Even under a Republican Senate in 2018-2020, several of Trump's Fed nominees failed, including Judy Shelton, Steve Moore and Marvin Goodfriend, and Skanda Amarnath expects even more scrutiny now.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: This precedent suggests that unconventional or partisan Fed picks are now close to impossible to confirm.

insights.claim: Divided government makes it harder to pass policy, especially in a crisis. The 2018 midterms were followed 18 months later by the COVID CARES Act, which needed heavy coordination, so a crisis response under this Congress is uncertain.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: If a shock hits, the fiscal response may be slower or smaller, which raises left-tail risk.

insights.claim: As a tail scenario, Senate Republicans from farm states west of the Mississippi, where tariff costs hit hardest and where even John Thune likely dislikes aggressive tariffs, could join Democrats to limit the president's executive power over trade. It would take a substantial number of Republican defections.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: A low-probability catalyst for rolling back tariffs, which would benefit farm exporters and importers.

insights.claim: Texas swung Democratic across every statewide office, including comptroller, lieutenant governor and the education board, which undercuts the pitch to corporations that Texas is the perfect business environment, a pitch that includes its new business court built to compete with Delaware for incorporations.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Companies that moved or reincorporated to Texas for political friendliness now face policy uncertainty; Skanda Amarnath calls this the most underrated surprise.
insights.quote: Texas is the perfect business environment. It's like, well, conditions can change.

insights.claim: California voters rejected the billionaire wealth tax, and Proposition 42, a billionaire-backed measure that prohibits new taxes on personal property such as business holdings, intellectual property and financial assets, was winning by a wide margin.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: California may be locking in protection against wealth taxes, which lowers tax risk for founders and asset holders there.

insights.claim: Prediction markets show Jon Ossoff moving into the lead for the 2028 Democratic nomination on the strength of his winning margin, while the field (including Andy Beshear and Josh Shapiro) is large and flat with no obvious front-runner. Skanda Amarnath doubts a democratic socialist ends up on the ticket.
insights.speaker: Skanda Amarnath
insights.so_what: Democrats leaning toward electability over ideology lowers the odds of a sharply anti-business platform in 2028.

insights.claim: Tracy Alloway compares the 2026 sweep to the post-Watergate Democratic landslide, since both pair high inflation with a deeply unpopular president, and she warns that Reagan took office about eight years later.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Regime shifts driven by inflation can reverse quickly, so be careful about extrapolating the new political map into long-dated positions.

insights.claim: The hosts argue that tech money is consistently ineffective at political giving, with no intuition for which races matter or how to spend well. They cite John Arnold's line that political giving is the original wealth tax, and suggest Elon Musk's political spending may turn out to be a colossal waste.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Do not price in political protection bought by tech billionaires' donations, which may get little in return.
insights.quote: political giving is the original wealth tax
